track.name: cybersecurity
track.label: Cybersecurity & Risk
track.summary: Go from the CIA triad and common attack types to risk assessments, compliance frameworks, and incident response — the security literacy every role in a modern organization increasingly needs.

phases.title: Security Fundamentals & Threat Landscape
phases.description: The core vocabulary and mental models of security — what you're protecting, from whom, and how attackers actually get in.

phases.title: Network & Application Security Basics
phases.description: How networks and web applications get attacked, and the baseline defenses and coding habits that stop the most common attacks.

phases.title: Identity, Access & Data Protection
phases.description: Who gets access to what, how encryption actually protects data, and what data privacy means in practice.

phases.title: Risk Assessment & Compliance Frameworks
phases.description: How organizations size up their risk and prove to auditors, customers, and regulators that they're managing it.

phases.title: Incident Response & Business Continuity
phases.description: What happens when prevention fails: detecting, containing, and recovering from an incident, then getting better at it.

phases.title: Security Culture & Applied Practice
phases.description: Turning security from a rulebook into something people actually do, plus hands-on labs to make the concepts stick.

topics.title: CIA Triad & Core Security Concepts
topics.description: Confidentiality, integrity, and availability — the three-part lens security people use to evaluate almost everything.

steps.d: Write what it means if your organization lost confidentiality on customer data (leaked email, exposed API key, a copy walked out the door).
Write what it means if data was modified without authorization (invoice amount changed, customer address altered, audit trail faked).
Write what it means if a critical system was inaccessible for one hour (cost of downtime, customer impact, recovery effort).
List five assets your organization depends on (database, email, website, financial system) and rate each for CIA sensitivity: 1-5 for each.
For the asset you scored highest on CIA, write what you'd do in the first 30 minutes if all three (confidentiality, integrity, availability) were compromised.

topics.title: Common Threats & Attack Types
topics.description: Malware, ransomware, and the other attack categories that show up in almost every breach report.

steps.d: Name and define the six main attack types: malware, ransomware, phishing, denial of service, privilege escalation, and data exfiltration.
For each threat type, list two or three preventive or detective controls that reduce the risk.
Find a public breach disclosure or incident report and map what happened to the threat categories (which attack type, which system, which defense failed).
For one system you use regularly, estimate which of the six threat types poses the highest risk and why.
For your highest-risk threat, describe one concrete change (policy, tool, training) that would reduce the likelihood or impact.

topics.title: Social Engineering & Phishing
topics.description: Why humans, not firewalls, are the easiest way into most organizations.

steps.d: Find or create a phishing attempt and mark every element (sender, urgency, request, link, attachment) that's designed to trick someone.
With your security team's permission, send a test phishing email to a small group and measure who clicks or replies; don't shame anyone.
List five pretexts an attacker might use to trick employees (IT support, new vendor, executive emergency, survey, prize).
Read a case study or watch a talk by a security researcher describing how they got inside using social engineering.
Propose one specific change to your email, training, or incident response process that would reduce successful phishing.

topics.title: Network Security Fundamentals
topics.description: Firewalls, VPNs, and the basic architecture decisions that keep a network from being wide open.

steps.d: Sketch your network boundaries: internet-facing servers, internal systems, database tier, and employee network zones.
Name every way data or people enter or leave your network (internet, VPN, third-party connections, removable media, wireless).
For each access point, describe what rules a firewall should enforce (which traffic in, which out, what to log).
Explain why a remote employee needs a VPN to access internal systems and what it does that public internet doesn't.
Talk to your IT team and describe how your actual network differs from the ideal (firewall rules, segmentation, controls).

topics.title: Web Application Security (OWASP Top 10)
topics.description: The ten vulnerability categories responsible for the vast majority of web app breaches.

steps.d: Read the current OWASP Top 10 list and choose two vulnerabilities you understand (injection, broken auth, XSS, etc.) and describe the attack.
Look at sample vulnerable code (from OWASP or a tutorial) and identify the bug that could let an attacker exploit it.
Take a web app you use and describe how you'd try to break in (bypass login, steal data, deface it, make it unavailable).
Find a CVE or bug bounty report for a real web app and trace the attack from first step through impact.
For one of the Top 10 vulnerabilities, describe a code practice or testing step that would prevent it (e.g., input validation, prepared statements, CSP).

topics.title: Secure Coding Basics
topics.description: Writing code that doesn't hand attackers an opening, using checklists instead of guesswork.

steps.d: Name ten security-critical mistakes developers make (hardcoded secrets, no input validation, weak crypto, SQL injection, race conditions).
Review sample code from a tutorial and identify which coding mistakes are present (don't need to fix it, just name them).
Write a 10-item checklist for developers to run before committing: input validation, secrets, auth, logging, error handling, etc.
For one application, list the entry points (APIs, inputs, files), trust boundaries, and data flows, then ask 'what could go wrong' at each.
Take real code you have access to (or a tutorial sample) and audit it against one security checklist item (e.g., no hardcoded secrets).

topics.title: Knowing What You Have: Asset Inventory
topics.description: You cannot protect or risk-assess what you have not listed — building and keeping an inventory of systems, data and dependencies.

steps.d: Write down what counts as yours: owned hardware, cloud accounts, SaaS you pay for, data stores, and anything internet-facing.

steps.t: Inventory one subnet or one cloud account
steps.d: List every host or service with its owner, purpose and whether it is reachable from outside. Start small and finish it.

steps.t: Classify by what breaks without it
steps.d: Mark each asset critical, important or standard based on what stops if it is gone. This is what later risk work prioritises on.
Pick a critical application and trace what it reads from and writes to. That chain is its blast radius.
Name the moment the inventory gets updated — a procurement step, a deploy step, a monthly review. A stale inventory is worse than none.

topics.title: Identity & Access Management
topics.description: Making sure the right people, and only the right people, can get to the right systems.

steps.d: For your organization, name the different permission levels (admin, user, read-only, contractor, guest) and what each can do.
Take your major systems and build a table: roles (engineer, manager, support, finance) and their access to each system (yes/no/limited).
Find one role that has more access than they need for their job (e.g., an engineer with admin on the finance system).
For over-provisioned roles, describe which accesses should be revoked and what happens if you revoke them.
Pull the access list from one critical system and identify any users who shouldn't have their current level.

topics.title: Encryption Fundamentals
topics.description: How data gets scrambled so it's useless without the key, and why there are two very different ways to do it.

steps.d: Describe the difference between symmetric (one key) and asymmetric (public/private) encryption with a real example for each.
For five scenarios (secure file transfer, password storage, credit card in database, HTTPS, signing a contract), pick symmetric or asymmetric and why.
For one critical system you use, document where encryption keys are stored, who can access them, and what the rotation interval is.
Look at sample code using encryption and spot mistakes (weak cipher, bad key storage, no authentication, wrong mode).
For a tool that claims encryption (VPN, password manager, file storage), research whether it actually uses strong encryption and manages keys properly.

topics.title: Data Privacy & Protection
topics.description: What organizations owe the people whose data they hold, and the regulations that make it enforceable.

steps.d: Name what personal data your organization holds (email, phone, location, financial, health, age) and which regulations apply (GDPR, CCPA, HIPAA, PCI-DSS).
For one type of personal data (customer email), document where it's collected, stored, processed, shared, and when it's deleted.
Pick one privacy regulation (GDPR, CCPA, HIPAA) and summarize the top three requirements in plain language.
Compare your current data practices to a regulation and list three ways you're not in compliance (or verify you are).
Draft or review a privacy policy statement covering: what data you collect, why, how you protect it, who has access, and how users can request deletion.

topics.title: Risk Assessment Fundamentals
topics.description: Turning 'what could go wrong' into a ranked, defensible list of what to fix first.

steps.d: Write the formula: risk = likelihood × impact, and describe a high-risk scenario (likely AND high-impact) and a low-risk one.
List 15-20 things that could go wrong in your organization (breach, data loss, fraud, compliance violation, vendor failure, physical theft).
Rate each risk on likelihood (1-5: unlikely to certain) and impact (1-5: low to critical), multiply to get a risk score.
Sort by risk score and identify your top 10 risks; ensure you have a mitigation plan for at least the top five.
Pick a risk you ranked low and argue why it might actually be higher; or pick one ranked high and argue for lower.

topics.title: Compliance Frameworks (SOC 2, ISO 27001, NIST)
topics.description: The frameworks auditors and customers actually check against, and what each one is really asking for.

steps.d: Look up SOC 2 Type II and NIST Cybersecurity Framework and write the main difference (one for compliance, one for risk management).
Find a plain-language summary of ISO 27001 and list five of its requirements (information classification, access control, incident response, etc.).
Pick one framework and find its control on password policy; write what it requires (complexity, length, rotation, MFA, etc.).
Take one compliance framework relevant to your organization and rate yourself on 5-10 of its key controls (compliant/not compliant/partial).
For the three biggest gaps you found, write a mitigation plan: what you'll do, who's responsible, and when it'll be done.

topics.title: Third-Party & Vendor Risk
topics.description: Your security posture is only as strong as the vendors and suppliers you've given access to.

steps.d: Name your top 10 third parties by risk and access level (cloud provider, SaaS, payment processor, data processor, contractor with network access).
Pick your riskiest vendor and reach out requesting their security documentation: certifications, incident history, data handling practices.
For three vendors, rate their risk: security certifications, incident history, access level, financial stability, contract terms.
For your highest-risk vendor, ask specific questions: Where is data stored? How is it encrypted? Who can access it? What's your incident response time?
Write a security clause for a new vendor contract that requires: SOC 2 or ISO 27001, data residency, breach notification, audit rights, incident response SLA.

topics.title: Incident Response Fundamentals
topics.description: The phases of handling a security incident, from first alert to closing the loop.

steps.d: Write what your organization will do in each phase: Preparation (tools ready), Detection (alert raised), Containment (stop the spread), Eradication (remove the threat), Recovery (restore systems), Post-Incident (learn).
For one threat type (data breach, ransomware, DDoS, insider threat), write step-by-step actions for the first four hours.
Assign roles for an incident: incident commander, lead investigator, legal counsel, communications, customer support, executive sponsor.
Run a tabletop exercise: describe a breach scenario and walk the team through their first response steps (detection, containment, communication, escalation).
After any actual incident (even minor), write down what happened, what worked, what didn't, and one improvement to make for next time.

topics.title: Business Continuity & Disaster Recovery
topics.description: Keeping the business running, and getting systems back, when something actually goes wrong.

steps.d: List the 5-10 systems your organization would be crippled without for one week (email, website, payment processing, HR, customer database).
For each critical system, calculate the cost of one hour of downtime (lost revenue, recovery effort, customer impact, brand damage).
For your top critical system, write how you'd restore it from scratch: backups needed, deployment time, data validation, communication.
Regularly attempt to restore a backup to a test system to verify it works; if it fails, fix it now instead of in an emergency.
For each critical system, state your Recovery Time Objective (how fast must it come back) and Recovery Point Objective (how much data loss is acceptable).

topics.title: Tabletop Exercises & Post-Incident Review
topics.description: Rehearsing the incident response plan before you need it, then honestly reviewing what happened after.

steps.d: Write a realistic incident scenario (a phishing attack gets one employee's credentials; they're used to access customer data) with enough detail to run a 1-hour exercise.
Gather 6-8 people from security, ops, legal, comms, and leadership; walk them through your scenario and have them describe actions in real time.
In the exercise, measure how long it takes to detect, notify stakeholders, start containment, and begin investigation.
Ask: What surprised you? What was unclear? What communication broke down? What would you do differently? Write down three improvements.
Take one finding from your exercise and implement it: a new tool, a clarified procedure, a trained role, or updated contact list.

topics.title: Building a Security-Aware Culture
topics.description: Turning security from an annual training video into habits people actually keep.

steps.d: List the security training your organization currently gives (onboarding, phishing, password hygiene, compliance) and who gets what.
Interview five employees across roles and ask them what they'd do if they got a phishing email or saw suspicious network activity.
For the biggest gap you found, design a 10-minute training: scenario, learning objective, quiz question, and one concrete action to remember.
Deploy one automated security reminder (Slack message, screensaver, team meeting agenda item) and measure weekly exposure rate across staff.
Before and after a security campaign (training, reminder, incentive), measure behavior: phishing click rate, password changes, MFA adoption, incident reports.

topics.title: Security for Non-Technical Teams
topics.description: The handful of things every employee, not just IT, needs to know and do.

steps.d: Name six things every employee (not just IT) must know: strong passwords, phishing, MFA, public WiFi risk, USB security, incident reporting.
Explain in plain language why complexity matters, why reuse is dangerous, and when (not just if) to change a password.
Describe what multi-factor authentication does, why it matters, and how to use it on one service they actually use.
Send a safe, non-punitive phishing simulation to your organization; report results honestly and offer retraining without blame.
Make reporting a breach suspicion easy: one click, one form, no shame; then confirm receipt and close the loop on their report.

topics.title: Hands-On Practice (CTFs & Labs)
topics.description: Free, legal environments to practice the attacker's side and see how the concepts hold up.

steps.d: Locate free legal cyber-range environments (HackTheBox, TryHackMe, PicoCTF, OverTheWire) and work through one beginner exercise.
Pick one Capture The Flag challenge and work through it: find vulnerabilities, exploit them, and extract the flag (without cheating).
After completing a CTF, write down the vulnerability you exploited, why it worked, how it applied to real systems, and how to fix it.
For one attack you practiced, reverse it: write the control that would detect or prevent it in a real system.
After completing five beginner challenges, attempt a medium-difficulty CTF or sandbox lab and document what you learn.
